lesson.title: First Introductions
lesson.subtitle: ich heiße ↔ hight, ich komme aus, ich wohne — the first sentences Germans actually speak

hook.title: Hight: the Verb You Already Owned
hook.content: Every German course opens with ich heiße — and the verb is an heirloom. Heißen descends from Proto-Germanic *haitaną, 'to call, to be called', and English wore the same verb until Shakespeare's day: archaic hight meant 'is called' — 'a city hight Rome'. Sir Gawain is hight so; your name is heißt so. The rest of the introduction kit is equally old: ich komme aus England (come, already yours), ich wohne in Berlin (the live/reside verb — no English twin, an honest memorize), ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt (and Jahr is the exact twin of year). Four formulas, all cognate-tested, and you can introduce yourself for a full minute.

footnotes.title: behest: the Command Sibling
footnotes.content: Heißen's family survives in English 'behest' — a bidding or command, literally a 'be-called'. The king's behest is what he calls you to do. Same *haitaną root as heißen, hight, and German Heißt du...?

pattern.title: The Four Formulas
pattern.content: 1. Ich heiße Anna. — 'I am called Anna'; question form: Wie heißt du? (informal) / Wie heißen Sie? (formal). 2. Ich komme aus England. — come from; most countries take aus with no article: aus Deutschland; feminine and plural countries keep theirs: aus der Schweiz. 3. Ich wohne in Berlin. — reside; city = bare in, country = in + dative: in Deutschland, in der Schweiz. 4. Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt. — literally 'I am twenty years old', word for word English. Stack them and the self-introduction builds itself: Ich heiße Anna. Ich komme aus England, und ich wohne jetzt in Berlin.
pattern.linguist_note: Heißen and hight share the s of *haitaną's present stem — heißt keeps it, hight wore it down. The question 'Wie heißen Sie?' literally asks 'How are you called?', the same logic as archaic 'How are you hight?' — both languages asking for a name by way of a calling.

exercises.prompt: Match each introduction formula with its literal reading:

matching_pairs.english: I am called (= my name is)
The oil is in the bag
matching_pairs.german: Das Öl ist in der Tüte

exercises.target_answer: Ich heiße, Ich komme aus, Ich wohne in, Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt, Das Öl ist in der Tüte, Herr Braun wohnt hier
exercises.meaning: my name is, I come from, I live in, I am twenty years old, the oil is in the bag, Mister Braun lives here
exercises.explanation: heißen = to be called (hight's twin); wohnen = to reside, with wo as its first syllable; jahr = the year you count yourself in. The age formula is word-for-word English — years old = Jahre alt. The nouns arrive next: Herr in front of the surname, die Fabrik where you work, das Gymnasium where you studied, die Rente, der Dom, die Art, die Kaution and eventuell already in your pocket.

exercises.meaning: Ich komme aus Deutschland = I come from Germany
exercises.explanation: aus = out of — origins run through the out-of preposition, and most countries stand bare: aus Deutschland (but aus der Schweiz keeps its article).

exercises.prompt: Which archaic English word is the twin of 'heiße'?
exercises.explanation: 'A city hight Rome' = 'a city is called Rome' — same *haitaną, same meaning, one s worn away.

exercises.prompt: 'Jahr' is the exact twin of which English word?
exercises.explanation: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt — 'I am twenty years old' — with Jahr/year the twin it has been for two thousand years.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German sentence for 'My name is Anna and I come from Berlin':
exercises.target_answer: Ich heiße Anna und ich komme aus Berlin
exercises.meaning: Ich heiße Anna und ich komme aus Berlin

vocab_hints.note: ich heiße = my name is — the hight twin

exercises.explanation: Two verb-second clauses joined by und — each clause holds its own verb in position 2, the rule from topic 14 already at work.

summary.outcome: Introduce yourself with heiße, komme aus, wohne in and the age formula — and explain the heißen/hight twin.

use_example.german: Ich heiße Anna. Ich komme aus England, und ich wohne in Berlin.
use_example.english: My name is Anna. I come from England, and I live in Berlin.

summary.takeaway: heißen ↔ hight ('to be called'), kommen aus (origins), wohnen in (residence), Jahre alt (age, word for word) — the whole first minute is cognate-built.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the alphabet — W is 'veh', V is 'fow', Z is 'tsett', and buchstabieren spells your name out loud.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We be called (twin: hight) here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir heißen heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in First Introductions.

heißen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *haitaną — archaic English hight 'was named' is the verified cognate (also behest). [wiktionary]

wohnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from the 'wish, love' root; no English cognate named on Wiktionary. [wiktionary]

alt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *aldaz — the twin of old; the l stayed, the vowel and final d/t report the shift. [wiktionary]

jahr.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *jār — the twin of English year. [wiktionary]

herr.context_translation: The gentleman is called Mr. Müller.
herr.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hairaz 'grey' — the grey-haired one, cognate with English hoar. [wiktionary]

öl.context_phrase: Ich brate das Ei in Öl.
öl.context_translation: I fry the egg in oil.
öl.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic oli, meaning olive oil, ultimately from Latin oleum; English oil descends from the same early Latin loan into Old English. [wiktionary]

tüte.etymology_derivation: From Low German tute, a conical bag — the page lists English tote as the cognate: the bag you tote things in. [wiktionary]

fabrik.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin fabrica — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Fabrik = FACTORY. (Fabric: der Stoff.) [wiktionary]

gymnasium.etymology_derivation: Both from the Greek wrestling-ground — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: das Gymnasium = ACADEMIC HIGH SCHOOL. (Gym: die Turnhalle.) [wiktionary]

rente.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin rendere — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Rente = PENSION. (Apartment rent: die Miete.) [wiktionary]

dom.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin domus (church-house) — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: der Dom = CATHEDRAL. (Dome: die Kuppel.) [wiktionary]

art.context_phrase: Diese Art von Buch ist gut.
art.context_translation: This kind of book is good.
art.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin ars/artis — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Art = KIND/TYPE. (Fine art: die Kunst.) [wiktionary]

kaution.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin cautio — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Kaution = SECURITY DEPOSIT. (Caution: die Vorsicht.) [wiktionary]

eventuell.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin eventus — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: eventuell = POSSIBLY. (Eventually: schließlich/am Ende.) [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
